clinician.trajectory_summary: A 69-year-old male presented with severe memory impairment, initially diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease based on an HDS-R score of 16 and a CT showing suspected dilatation of the right lateral ventricle. He had a history of significant psychological trauma, including witnessing his wife swept away by a tsunami and strained family relationships. Despite general memory loss, he denied depressive feelings, could recount a traumatic event in detail, and maintained daily activities like driving and interacting with acquaintances (E002). Later, after an emotional fight with his son, he demonstrated significant memory improvement, recalling details accurately (E004). This fluctuating memory, along with the absence of depressive mood, led clinicians to consider his memory impairment as continuing dissociation resulting from serious psychological trauma and family separation, effectively ruling out depression (E007) and implicitly re-evaluating the initial Alzheimer's diagnosis.
